drug_class: RNA interference (RNAi) therapy / small interfering RNA (siRNA)
purpose: Patisiran is used to treat adults with a rare inherited disease called hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis (hATTR amyloidosis), which causes nerve damage. This condition happens when an abnormal protein called transthyretin builds up and damages nerves throughout the body. This medicine helps slow down or improve the nerve problems caused by this disease.
how_it_works: Your body has a gene that makes a protein called transthyretin (TTR). In people with this disease, that gene makes a faulty version of the protein that clumps together and damages nerves. Patisiran works by 'silencing' the instructions your liver uses to make that harmful protein, so much less of it is produced. Think of it like turning down the volume on a broken signal — less bad protein means less damage to your nerves.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include infusion-related reactions during or after the IV drip, such as flushing, feeling sick to your stomach, stomach pain, back pain, shortness of breath, headache, or feeling dizzy. Some people also experience tiredness, swelling in the legs or feet, or runny nose. Most of these are mild to moderate.
warnings: Before each infusion, you will be given premedications (like steroids and antihistamines) to help prevent infusion reactions — it is very important not to skip these. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as the safety in pregnancy is not fully known. Let your healthcare team know about all your other medications, including supplements. Because this medicine lowers vitamin A levels in your blood, your doctor will likely recommend a vitamin A supplement while you are on this treatment. Do not stop treatment without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: Patisiran is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion — meaning it goes directly into a vein — once every 3 weeks. The dose is based on your body weight. Each infusion usually takes about 80 minutes, and you will receive it at a clinic or infusion center. You will be given premedications about 60 minutes before your infusion to help prevent reactions.
